title: The Fretboard
intro: Every fret is a semitone and every string is a fourth (or, G to B, a major third) above the one below. From those two facts you can find any note, and a handful of octave shapes link the same note across the whole neck.

blocks.text: Each string runs up the chromatic scale from its open note, one semitone per fret: the low E string is E (open), F (1), F♯ (2), G (3), G♯ (4), A (5), A♯ (6), B (7), C (8), C♯ (9), D (10), D♯ (11), E (12). At fret 12 the pattern starts again an octave higher. Remember the natural notes with no sharp between them, E–F and B–C, exactly as on the piano (see Notation (#/arts/music-theory/sound-and-pitch/notation)).

items: Low E string (6): G at 3, A at 5, C at 8, D at 10, E at 12.
A string (5): B at 2, C at 3, D at 5, E at 7, G at 10, A at 12.
Learn the natural notes on strings 6 and 5 first: they hold the roots of almost every movable chord.

blocks.alt: A guitar neck drawn horizontally with the high e string on top and frets 0 to 12. Every natural note is a labelled blue dot (C in red) and the sharps are small grey labels; fret 12 repeats the open-string names.
blocks.caption: Every note in the first 12 frets. Natural notes are labelled; the C's are red so you can see how one note repeats across the neck.

blocks.text: The same note one octave up, found from a root:

items: From string 6 or 5: two strings up and two frets higher (A on string 6 fret 5 → A on string 4 fret 7).
From string 4 or 3: two strings up and three frets higher (because the octave crosses the G–B major third): G on string 4 fret 5 → G on string 2 fret 8.
From string 6 to string 1 at the same fret: two octaves.
Twelve frets up the same string.

blocks.text: The same pitch on the next string down is five frets back (four back on the G string going to the B): A on string 6 fret 5 equals the open A string. These are the tuning reference points, and the reason a phrase can be moved across strings to stay in one position.

Middle C (C4) is on string 2 fret 1, string 3 fret 5, string 4 fret 10, string 5 fret 15 and string 6 fret 20. Guitar music is written an octave above where it sounds, so the guitar's written middle C is played on string 5 fret 3, which actually sounds C3.

widget.title: One pitch, many places: C4 and E4

blocks.title: Find it
blocks.text: Where are the two lowest D pitches on the neck in standard tuning?
solution: The guitar's lowest note is E2, so there is no D2. The lowest D is D3, found in three places: open string 4, string 5 fret 5 and string 6 fret 10.
The next is D4: string 2 fret 3, string 3 fret 7, string 4 fret 12 and string 5 fret 17 (and string 6 fret 22 on a 24-fret neck).
blocks.answer: D3 (open 4th string, 5th string fret 5, 6th string fret 10) and D4 (4th string fret 12, 3rd string fret 7, 2nd string fret 3)

blocks.title: Octave
blocks.text: Your root is B♭ on string 5 fret 1. Where is the B♭ an octave up using an octave shape?
solution: From string 5: two strings up (string 3), two frets higher: string 3 fret 3 = B♭3.

blocks.text: Sources: Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press.
